items_missed: No agenda statement and no 'sound good?'. The open was 'Einstein moving this is Dana. Can I have your name?' then straight to 'how can I help you?'. The customer never got a roadmap or a timeframe — on a call that ran 23.8 minutes for a one-bedroom apartment, telling her up front 'I'll gather details, then walk you through pricing, about 10-15 minutes' would have set expectations for the length.
Never asked 'how are you today?' — went from name capture directly to 'how can I help you?'

No booking attempt. This is the biggest miss on the call. Danah confirmed availability herself in the first two minutes ('September 19th let's see. Yup. Saturday. Okay, great. We still have availability'), ran a complete intake, and closed with the passive 'if you wanna go ahead and move forward, just let us know.' A qualified, warm, no-deposit-required customer with a confirmed open date was never asked to book.

Storage stops and additional stops never asked about, even though the customer volunteered a multi-destination picture on her own — 'items that are going to be donated to goodwill' and 'some that are going to be put in the dumpster' — which is exactly the moment to confirm nothing needs a truck stop.

Clock start never explained. She covered the 2.5-hour minimum and 15-minute increments but never said the clock starts on-site when the contract opens — a gap that matters on this specific job because there is a 30-40 minute San Antonio to San Marcos drive the customer may assume is billed differently.
What's-included list was partial: 'there is gas in the truck taxes and insurance. We will also wrap all of your furniture.' Pads, bands, and tools were never named.

Save Your Ass prep speech never delivered. The only gesture at it was 'it'll all depends how on how well prepared you are on moving day and you pay for the actual time' — the cost link without a single actionable tip. No consolidation examples (loose items in drawers, photos off walls, kids' toys boxed), no 'take a carload' tip. The customer had explicitly said she is packing herself next week and asked for guidance — she was primed to receive this and got nothing.

Walk distance was measured carefully at both ends (10 feet to the curb at origin, 20 feet from the stairs to the unit, ~40 feet of hallway at destination) but then never cited as a driver when the estimate was built. The estimate rationale named only special items, the second-floor-to-second-floor stairs, and drive time.
Truck count never stated. 'Two movers' was given repeatedly; the customer was never told one truck.

Estimate was deliberately padded on request rather than defended. Danah modeled 2.5-4 hours, then when the customer said 'I would prefer to estimate on the higher because I could be wrong,' Danah answered 'I'll just put in, we'll over estimate it a little bit just to be on the safer side. Yes, I would estimate it to take about four and a half hours' — then wrote something different again ('I'll just put in about three and a half to four and a half hours'). Three different numbers in ninety seconds, and the one going in EMMA is inflated on customer preference, not on job facts.

No BOLDED-details framing for the confirmation email and no explicit 'reply with any corrections' — the closest was the softer 'any changes that you have Sarah, just let us know so we can update the profile here.'
Hours and how to reach us never given. Every callback instruction was the vague 'just let us know.'

Ecobox referral missed on a clear opening. The customer said 'I didn't know what size boxes to use if you all want cause I know when I went to the store they had small, medium and large.' Danah answered with sizing advice for kitchen items and linens but never mentioned Ecobox or where to source boxes.

Roughly five minutes spent reading back a 2019 inventory from an old profile under the customer's ex-husband's name, item by item, only to conclude 'Yeah. Okay then we can just disregard this profile then.' The customer had already said 'I've been getting rid of a lot of things' before the read-back started.
top_strength: The stressor probe and the specialty-item handling were genuinely excellent, and they came in the right order. Before pricing anything, Danah asked 'before we talk about your move and before I start building your estimate, do you have any like concerns or anything important for you that you wanna talk about for about the move' — and that one question surfaced the entire risk profile of the job: a hundred-year-old Tuttle sewing machine the customer had watched previous movers wheel instead of lift, a chest freezer, and a fragile electric piano. She then qualified the sewing machine for weight ('Do you think it's above 300 pounds or 500 pounds?'), committed to documenting it ('I will let the movers and I'll put in a note here. So whenever you book with us our crew are prepared and they'll know what to do with the sewing machine'), and answered the freezer with the disconnect/reconnect service. She followed that immediately with an unprompted trust builder — 'we don't hire a daily contracted workers. So all our crew, all our movers are employed with background checks and a regular professional training' — and then the cleanest No Worries explanation in this batch, correctly framed against the industry baseline: 'up to $2,000 per move to repair, replace or reimburse any accidental damage. So unlike other moving companies, they will either charge you for extra or the offer only the state mandated 60 cents per pound coverage.' When the customer asked to read the actual coverage language, Danah did not deflect — she tied it to the email handoff. She also read the rate tier proactively when asked, giving both Saturday ($206) and Monday ($192) so the customer could make her own call. Probing was near-complete: both full addresses, floors at both ends, elevators at both ends, bonus rooms, packing, and a box count she coached out of a customer who did not have one, using the right technique ('typically one bedroom apartment has fifteen to 25 boxes usually. So do you think you'd be within that range over or under?'). The school-bus equivalent showed up too.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: ask for the booking. Danah did almost everything needed to earn this move and then let it walk. She personally confirmed September 19 was open in the first two minutes, ran a thorough 20-minute intake, explained No Worries better than most of the team, and told the customer 'we don't require deposit to book' — and then closed with 'if you wanna go ahead and move forward, just let us know.' The line she needed, right after the no-deposit mention, was: 'Sarah, September 19th is open right now and there's no deposit to hold it — want me to lock that Saturday in for you while we're on the phone? If anything changes with the box count or the date, we just update it, no penalty.' Every objection was already handled; there was nothing left to overcome but the ask. Second priority, and this one is a company-level issue, not just a Danah issue: she let the customer set the estimate. Her own model said 2.5-4 hours. The customer asked to inflate it because a third party is reimbursing, and Danah said 'we'll over estimate it a little bit just to be on the safer side,' floated 4.5 hours out loud, then wrote 3.5-4.5. That is a padded number entering EMMA for a stated reason that has nothing to do with the job — and it is the exact behavior that keeps estimate accuracy stuck in the 40s. The right move is to hold the honest range and explain the mechanics that protect her: 'Sarah, my honest estimate is 3 to 4 hours, and I'd rather give your husband's company a number we'll actually hit. Here's why you're protected either way — the clock starts on-site when we open the contract and you only pay for the actual time, in 15-minute increments after the 2.5-hour minimum. So if we finish in 3, that's what you're billed. If you want a ceiling for the reimbursement paperwork, I'll note 4 hours as the outside case and show both.' Same reassurance, no fabricated hours. Worth flagging for the estimate-accuracy work: this is a live example of the pressure that inflates apartment and small-move estimates, coming from the customer side rather than the manager side. Third: the prep speech. The customer said she is boxing next week and asked what size boxes to use — a wide-open door for both Save Your Ass and an Ecobox referral, and neither came through. 'Since you're packing yourself, here's how you shave real money off the bill: get everything small into boxes, empty the drawers, take the photos off the walls, and take one carload of the fragile odds and ends yourself. Every trip up and down those stairs the crew doesn't have to make is time off your clock. Does that make sense?' Fourth, and quick: Meet Your Mover and the On-Time Guarantee are both free to say and both went unsaid, and this customer in particular would have valued Meet Your Mover — she is a repeat customer whose specific complaint about her last crew was how they handled her antique. Last, a process note: five minutes went into reading back a 2019 inventory from a profile under the customer's ex-husband's name that was then discarded. Once she said 'I've been getting rid of a lot of things,' the faster path was to skip the read-back and build fresh.
phone_presence_notes: Consistently warm and attentive — used 'Sarah' well past the 3-time bar, responded to the unknown square footage with 'No worries, that's okay,' checked the spelling of her name rather than assuming ('Sarah is it with an H?'), and the customer stayed positive throughout and closed with 'well thank you so much' — though the acknowledgments leaned heavily on stacked 'Mm-hmm / Uh-huh / Yup' filler and long runs of 'Okay. Got it, okay. Alright' rather than varied language, and there was no humor or lightness anywhere in the call.
audio_review_reason: The quoted dollar figure came through the transcript as '$63,129,' which is impossible for a 2.5-4 hour two-mover job at $206/hr plus a $105 trip fee — the number the customer actually heard cannot be verified from text. Two other pricing phrases are garbled the same way ('free service zoom Bator fee' and 'no sterle fees'), so the trip-fee explanation and the no-hidden-fees list need an audio check. Also worth listening to the estimate-padding exchange directly, since three different hour ranges were spoken in about ninety seconds and it is unclear from text which one the customer believes is going in her email.
